Issues.Title: Track service-worker sources in Visual Studio’s fast up-to-date check
Issues.Body: # Track service-worker sources in Visual Studio’s fast up-to-date check ## Summary Register `@(ServiceWorker)` as an `UpToDateCheckInput` in the `StaticWebAssets` set when removing service-worker sources from `Content`. This allows Visual Studio’s fast up-to-date check to track development service-worker changes in existing PWA projects without requiring project-file or template changes. Addresses the SDK-owned portion of dotnet/aspnetcore#47388. Supersedes the template-only approach in dotnet/aspnetcore#69843. ### Root cause The PWA template declares `service-worker.js` using the custom `ServiceWorker` item: ```xml ``` However, the `ServiceWorker` item was not registered as an input to Visual Studio's fast up-to-date check. As a result, changing `service-worker.js` did not make the project appear out of date. Visual Studio could skip the build, leaving the previous service worker in the build output. A rebuild worked because it bypassed the up-to-date decision and rebuilt the project unconditionally. ### Before After changing `wwwroot/service-worker.js` and invoking Build: - Visual Studio could consider the project up to date. - The build could be skipped. - The service worker in the build output remained unchanged. - A full Rebuild was required to propagate the change. ### After After changing `wwwroot/service-worker.js`: - Visual Studio detects that a tracked build input changed. - The project is no longer incorrectly considered up to date. - Build runs and propagates the updated service worker to the build output. - A full Rebuild is no longer required. ## Changes - Track development service-worker sources alongside their removal from `Content`. - Leave publish-only `PublishedContent` sources out of the added build inputs. - Add regression tests that inspect actual design-time inputs: - Service-worker sources inside `wwwroot`. - Custom service-worker sources outside `wwwroot`. - Preservation of existing static-asset and explicitly registered inputs. - Exclusion of publish-only service-worker sources. - Unchanged input collection for non-PWA projects. - Document SDK ownership of service-worker up-to-date tracking. Service-worker generation and publish processing are unchanged. ## Validation Automated tests and Visual Studio validation have not been completed. Build/test execution was stopped at the contributor’s request. Planned focused regression command: ```powershell .\.dotnet\dotnet.exe scripts\RunTests.cs -- ` --project test\Microsoft.NET.Sdk.StaticWebAssets.Tests\Microsoft.NET.Sdk.StaticWebAssets.Tests.csproj ` --filter "FullyQualifiedName~CollectStaticWebAssetInputsDesignTime_" ` --test-binlogs

Issues.Title: Microsoft.DotNet.MSBuildSdkResolver throws ArgumentException: 'id' must be a valid path component (MSB4242) for project SDKs referenced by folder path in VS MSBuild
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

In Visual Studio 2026 (18.11), any project whose `Sdk` attribute is a folder path fails to evaluate under Visual Studio's `MSBuild.exe`. Examples: `<Project Sdk="$(MSBuildThisFileDirectory)..\MySdk">` or `<Import Project="Sdk.props" Sdk="C:\path\to\MySdk" />`. The error is MSB4242.

The workload part of `Microsoft.DotNet.MSBuildSdkResolver` passes the SDK name straight into `new WorkloadPackId(sdkReferenceName)` in `CachingWorkloadResolver.Resolve`. That constructor throws when the name isn't a single valid path component, and MSBuild treats a resolver that throws as a fatal error. So the default SDK resolver, which would resolve `<path>\Sdk\Sdk.props`, never gets a turn.

The same project evaluates and builds fine with `dotnet msbuild` / `dotnet build` (.NET SDK 10.0.403), where the default resolver runs first.

This also breaks tools that load VS MSBuild through MSBuildLocator, such as SlnGen from a developer prompt. It very likely breaks loading these projects in the VS IDE as well.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create this folder layout:
   ```
   repro\
     MySdk\
       Sdk\
         Sdk.props
         Sdk.targets
     App\
       App.csproj
   ```

2. `MySdk\Sdk\Sdk.props`:
   ```xml
   <Project>
     <Import Project="Sdk.props" Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk" />
   </Project>
   ```

3. `MySdk\Sdk\Sdk.targets`:
   ```xml
   <Project>
     <Import Project="Sdk.targets" Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk" />
   </Project>
   ```

4. `App\App.csproj`:
   ```xml
   <Project Sdk="$(MSBuildThisFileDirectory)..\MySdk">
     <PropertyGroup>
       <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
     </PropertyGroup>
   </Project>
   ```

5. From `repro\App`, run Visual Studio's MSBuild:
   ```powershell
   & "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\18\Professional\MSBuild\Current\Bin\amd64\MSBuild.exe" App.csproj -getProperty:TargetFramework -nologo
   ```

6. From the same folder, run the .NET SDK's MSBuild for comparison:
   ```powershell
   dotnet msbuild App.csproj -getProperty:TargetFramework -nologo
   ```

### Expected behavior

Both commands print `net10.0`. When the SDK name is a path, the resolver should return "not resolved" (or skip it) so the default SDK resolver can find `..\MySdk\Sdk\Sdk.props`. Folder-path SDK references are documented MSBuild behavior.

### Actual behavior

Step 6 (`dotnet msbuild`) prints `net10.0` and exits with 0.

Step 5 (VS MSBuild) exits with 1:

```
MSBUILD : error MSB4242: SDK Resolver Failure: "The SDK resolver "Microsoft.DotNet.MSBuildSdkResolver" failed while attempting to resolve the SDK "C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp\sdkpathrepro\App\..\MySdk". Exception: "System.ArgumentException: 'id' must be a valid path component
Parameter name: id
   at Microsoft.NET.Sdk.WorkloadMSBuildSdkResolver.CachingWorkloadResolver.Resolve(String sdkReferenceName, IWorkloadManifestProvider manifestProvider, IWorkloadResolver workloadResolver)
   at Microsoft.NET.Sdk.WorkloadMSBuildSdkResolver.CachingWorkloadResolver.Resolve(String sdkReferenceName, String dotnetRootPath, String sdkVersion, String userProfileDir, String globalJsonPath)
   at Microsoft.DotNet.MSBuildSdkResolver.DotNetMSBuildSdkResolver.Resolve(SdkReference sdkReference, SdkResolverContext context, SdkResultFactory factory)
   at Microsoft.Build.BackEnd.SdkResolution.SdkResolverService.TryResolveSdkUsingSpecifiedResolvers(...)""  ...\App\App.csproj
```

The same failure happens with:
- `<Sdk Name="C:\path\to\MySdk" />`
- `<Import Project="Sdk.props" Sdk="C:\path\to\MySdk" />`

### Is this a regression?

_No response_

### Are there any workarounds?

- Set `MSBuildEnableWorkloadResolver=false` before running VS MSBuild. The project then evaluates. This turns off workload SDK resolution for everything, so it isn't viable for projects that need workloads.
- Replace `Sdk="<path>"` with explicit `<Import Project="<path>\Sdk\Sdk.props" />` and `<Import Project="<path>\Sdk\Sdk.targets" />`.
- Use `dotnet build` / `dotnet msbuild` instead of VS MSBuild.

### dotnet --info output

```console

```

### IDE version

Visual Studio Professional 2026, 18.11.12328.437

### Other details

### Suspected cause

`src/Resolvers/Microsoft.NET.Sdk.WorkloadMSBuildSdkResolver/CachingWorkloadResolver.cs` calls:

```csharp
workloadResolver?.TryGetPackInfo(new WorkloadPackId(sdkReferenceName));
```

`WorkloadPackId`'s constructor throws `ArgumentException` when `PathComponentUtilities.IsValidPathComponent(id)` is false. Folder-path SDK names (containing `\`, `:`, `..`) should be checked with `IsValidPathComponent` before this call, or the exception caught, and the resolver should report "not resolved" so later resolvers can run.

### Environment

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| OS | Windows (x64) |
| Visual Studio | Visual Studio Professional 2026, 18.11.12328.437 |
| VS MSBuild | 18.11.1.51303 |
| Resolver used by VS MSBuild | `MSBuild\Current\Bin\SdkResolvers\Microsoft.DotNet.MSBuildSdkResolver\Microsoft.DotNet.MSBuildSdkResolver.dll`, FileVersion 10.4.326.52412, ProductVersion `10.0.403-servicing.26523.112+5a2162bea6845eabc1fc721624a43568c65db3b1` |
| .NET SDK (`dotnet --version`) | 10.0.403 (8.0.x and 10.0.114 also installed) |
| `global.json` | Not needed to reproduce |

Issues.Title: File-based app artifact cache grows without bound: keyed by source path, no cross-path sharing, and 30-day retention cannot keep up
Issues.Body:
## Summary

`dotnet run file.cs` places build output in a per-user cache directory
(`~/Library/Application Support/dotnet/runfile/` on macOS, `~/.local/share/dotnet/runfile/` on Linux)
under a subdirectory named by a hash of the entry point's **full source path**. Because the key is the
path and not the content, moving or copying a byte-identical app — or generating a fresh temporary tree
per test case — produces a new full artifact directory every time. There is no cross-path sharing, and
the documented cleanup cannot keep up.

I reproduced this on a clean tree with a five-line app. Observed cache growth: **755 GB in ~1,400
directories over two days**, 90% of the data volume. Most of it is not the user's app.

## Environment

```
.NET SDK 10.0.402
macOS 26 (arm64), APFS
GitHub.Copilot.SDK 1.0.26  (pulls the Copilot CLI runtime into the build output)
```

## Reproduction

The package reference is only there because it makes the per-run cost visible; the same cache-key
behaviour occurs with a plain `Console.WriteLine` app (see "Without any package" below).

```cs
// repro.cs
#:package GitHub.Copilot.SDK@1.0.26
Console.WriteLine("repro");
```

```bash
CACHE="$HOME/Library/Application Support/dotnet/runfile"

mkdir -p /tmp/rfr/a /tmp/rfr/b
cp repro.cs /tmp/rfr/a/ && cp repro.cs /tmp/rfr/b/   # byte-identical, sha256 verified

(cd /tmp/rfr/a && dotnet run repro.cs)   # cold: 4.4s
(cd /tmp/rfr/a && dotnet run repro.cs)   # warm: 0.14s
(cd /tmp/rfr/b && dotnet run repro.cs)   # cold again: 4.7s
```

Observed cache directories:

```
repro-552f7ca2…f4fdb   → /private/tmp/rfr/a/repro.cs.csproj
repro-16b02075…c46b95  → /private/tmp/rfr/b/repro.cs.csproj
```

Each is **546 MB**. Evidence they are physically separate copies, not shared storage:

```
$ stat -f 'inode=%i links=%l size=%z' \
    $CACHE/repro-552f7c…/obj/debug/copilot-cli/1.0.103/darwin-arm64/copilot.tgz \
    $CACHE/repro-16b020…/obj/debug/copilot-cli/1.0.103/darwin-arm64/copilot.tgz
inode=96355505 links=1 size=83944573 …/repro-552f7c…/copilot.tgz
inode=96356143 links=1 size=83944573 …/repro-16b020…/copilot.tgz

$ shasum -a 256 …/repro-552f7c…/copilot.tgz …/repro-16b020…/copilot.tgz
4cba81686f2d4a56e2ea2e1bd1cdde303d07f28de11593e1db1786f1219b8f74  …/repro-552f7c…/copilot.tgz
4cba81686f2d4a56e2ea2e1bd1cdde303d07f28de11593e1db1786f1219b8f74  …/repro-16b020…/copilot.tgz
```

Different inodes, `links=1`, identical bytes — two full copies of the same 84 MB archive, plus two full
copies of its extracted payload.

### Without any package

The keying and the lack of sharing are independent of the Copilot CLI:

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/p1 /tmp/p2
echo 'Console.WriteLine("hi");' > /tmp/p1/p.cs
cp /tmp/p1/p.cs /tmp/p2/p.cs
(cd /tmp/p1 && dotnet run p.cs)   # creates p-<hash of /tmp/p1/p.cs>
(cd /tmp/p2 && dotnet run p.cs)   # creates a second, different p-<hash>, no reuse
```

This second directory is small (~80 KB), so it is invisible in practice — but it demonstrates the
cache-key semantics are path-based for every file-based app.

## Why this matters here

The motivating workload is a test harness that must exercise an app against several source/deployment
variants. It builds each variant in its own temporary directory so the test can prove a guard rejects a
stale deployment. Each temporary tree is a new path, so each case costs a full cold build:

| Artifact origin | Directories | Size |
|---|---|---|
| Temporary test trees (fresh path per case) | 1,346 | 716 GB |
| Persistent worktrees | 48 | 18 GB |
| Main checkout | 20 | 11 GB |

That is a legitimate use of temporary directories, and it is the shape most likely to be hit by
CI-style harnesses and agent sandboxes.

## The cleanup does not help

Per the documented policy (`documentation/general/dotnet-run-file.md`, "Build outputs") artifacts are
cleaned every 2 days by a background task, removing entries unused for 30 days. That is correct
behaviour for a developer editing one file repeatedly, but it cannot bound a workload that mints new
paths faster than 30 days' worth of them expire:

```
$ dotnet clean file-based-apps
Scanning for folders to remove in: /Users/core/Library/Application Support/dotnet/runfile
Total folders removed: 0

$ dotnet clean file-based-apps --dry-run --days 0
Scanning for folders to remove in: /Users/core/Library/Application Support/dotnet/runfile
Would remove folders: 1550
```

Every entry was 0–2 days old, so nothing qualifies under the default cutoff. Two gaps make this
unrecoverable in practice:

1. The retention window is not configurable — the docs state that only the automatic cleanup can be
   disabled (`DOTNET_CLI_DISABLE_FILE_BASED_APP_ARTIFACTS_AUTOMATIC_CLEANUP=true`) and that "other
   parameters of the automatic cleanup are currently not configurable". `--days` exists only on the
   manual command.
2. There is no size ceiling. Nothing in the policy is expressed in bytes, so no amount of reuse can
   trigger reclamation.

The only recoverable signal is `dotnet clean file-based-apps --days 0`, which is not discoverable from
the docs and destroys the warm caches too.

## Related

- #49568 asks for the cache *location* to be redirectable. `#:property ArtifactsPath=` (or a
  `Directory.Build.props`) works and does keep output out of the cache, but it still leaves a ~84 KB
  stub directory per source path, and it does not address growth or sharing.
- #52773 reports the same path-keyed directory being a concurrency hazard.
- #48250 (closed by #49666) introduced the cleanup policy.

## Possible directions

I am not prescribing an implementation, but the axes seem to be:

1. **Content-addressed or package-identity-keyed caching** for restored/built dependencies, so
   identical inputs at different paths do not re-download or re-copy. The 84 MB archive and its
   extracted payload are the dominant cost and are identical across every entry.
2. **A size budget** for the cache as a whole, reclaiming least-recently-used entries once it is
   exceeded, so growth is bounded regardless of path churn.
3. **Documentation**: state the retention window and the `--days` option in "Build outputs", so a
   user facing an unbounded cache has a discoverable remedy short of deleting the directory.

## Impact

On this machine the cache reached 755 GB. It is safe to delete, but nothing in the CLI reports it and
the documented cleanup command reports "0 removed" while doing so, which reads as "nothing to clean".

Issues.Title: dotnetup: enumerate system installs without loading hostfxr
Issues.Body:
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/issues/56932

## Summary

Replace dotnetup's hostfxr-based system install discovery with a small on-disk enumerator, and delete the now-unused `HostFxrWrapper`.

- Walk `sdk/<version>` and `shared/<framework>/<version>` using one marker-file helper shared with `InstallationValidator`: `dotnet.dll` for SDKs and `<framework>.deps.json` for runtimes. Ignore invalid version names and folders without the appropriate marker.
- Do not load native libraries, set `HOSTFXR_PATH`, or require a muxer or `host/fxr` directory for discovery. Valid component folders in partial roots are now discoverable.
- Preserve system-root discovery, current-process architecture tagging/filtering, unknown-framework mapping, root-priority deduplication, descending version ordering, and on-disk folder versions. This does not introduce multilevel lookup or change `.version` interpretation.
- Retain per-root filesystem-failure warnings and telemetry, now named `system_install.enumeration_*` instead of `hostfxr.enumeration_*`.
- Update the two design references that described the removed hostfxr path.

Installation validation keeps its existing muxer requirements and Windows Desktop exception; only the component-marker check is shared. Architecture detection of the actual root is intentionally unchanged.

## Validation

- Focused `SystemInstallEnumeratorTests`, `InstallationValidatorTests`, and `InitWorkflowTests`: **44 passed, 2 non-Windows-only tests skipped**, no failures.
- Regression coverage includes missing and invalid hostfxr, all supported component markers, invalid versions, incorrect framework markers, unknown frameworks, missing/empty roots, folder-version preservation, and root-priority/version ordering.
- Built dotnetup, including its **Windows x64 NativeAOT publish**, with **0 warnings and 0 errors**.
- Changed-file formatting verification, `git diff --check`, and local Markdown link/anchor validation passed.

Tests were run through `scripts/RunTests.cs` with isolated artifacts. Validation was local on Windows; cross-platform execution is left to CI.

Issues.Title: dotnetup: enumerate system installs with the folder rules instead of loading hostfxr
Issues.Body:
Follow-up from https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/56913.

## Problem

`DotnetEnvironmentManager.GetExistingSystemInstalls` lists the SDKs and runtimes in each system install root by calling `HostFxrWrapper.getInstalls`, which loads the root's native hostfxr into the dotnetup process and calls `hostfxr_get_dotnet_environment_info`.

- [DotnetEnvironmentManager.cs](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/release/dnup/src/Installer/dotnetup.Library/DotnetEnvironmentManager.cs) (`GetExistingSystemInstalls`)
- [HostFxrWrapper.cs](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/release/dnup/src/Installer/Microsoft.Dotnet.Installation/Internal/HostFxrWrapper.cs) (`getInstalls`, `PreloadHostFxrLibrary`)

This has costs:

- **Native loading can fail.** It throws when `host/fxr` is missing or the loaded hostfxr doesn't export `hostfxr_get_dotnet_environment_info`. The failure is reported as a warning and the root is skipped.
- **Process-wide state.** On Unix, `PreloadHostFxrLibrary` sets `HOSTFXR_PATH` with `AppContext.SetData`, which carries over to later roots in the same process. On Windows, the first hostfxr loaded may serve every later call.
- **Two definitions of an install.** `InstallationValidator` already copies the host's rules for what counts as an install: an SDK folder with `dotnet.dll`, a framework folder with `<framework>.deps.json`. Listing system installs uses hostfxr instead, so the two can disagree.

## Proposal

Enumerate `sdk/*` and `shared/<framework>/*` under each system root with the same rules `InstallationValidator` uses, and remove the hostfxr dependency from this path. Keep one shared helper for "is this folder an install" so validation and listing can't drift apart.

## To check

- Whether anything else relies on hostfxr's view, such as how it treats multilevel lookup or install locations.
- Behavior when a root has no `host/fxr` (a partial install), which works with a folder walk but fails today.
- Architecture handling: `getInstalls` stamps every install with the current process architecture.

## Notes

- System installs report the on-disk folder version as `Version`. For RTM and servicing daily builds that differs from the build version, and `.version` can't recover it for runtimes. SDK `.version` line 4 holds the full build version even for stable releases (for example `10.0.403-servicing.26523.112`). This issue doesn't need to change that.

Issues.Title: Fix culture-sensitive analyzer path resolution in ResolvePackageAssets
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Fix culture-sensitive analyzer path resolution in ResolvePackageAssets.

When resolving Roslyn analyzer assets from NuGet packages, AnalyzerResolver.IsFileCompilerVersionSpecific attempts to parse compiler version subfolders (e.g. `/roslyn5.0/`) using `file.IndexOf(_compilerNameSearchString)`. Because no `StringComparison` was specified, it defaulted to `StringComparison.CurrentCulture` (linguistic search).

In cultures where `/` is treated as ignorable punctuation (such as Thai `th-TH`), `file.IndexOf("/roslyn")` skips the leading slash and matches at `r`, offsetting the version start index by 1 character. Subsequently, `file.IndexOf('/', compilerVersionStart)` starts searching from `.` (also ignorable punctuation in Thai collation), immediately matching at offset 0 and returning an empty string `""`.

As a result, `Version.TryParse("")` returns `false`, causing the SDK to treat all compiler-specific analyzers as version-agnostic and pass every Roslyn variant (`roslyn4.0` through `roslyn5.0`) to the compiler simultaneously, leading to `CS0111` / `CS0757` compilation errors on machines running under such cultures.

Specifying `StringComparison.Ordinal` ensures technical path delimiter matching is consistent across all machine cultures.

\\\diff
- int compilerNameStart = file.IndexOf(_compilerNameSearchString);
+ int compilerNameStart = file.IndexOf(_compilerNameSearchString, StringComparison.Ordinal);
\\\

## Evidence

- **Before (`th-TH` culture):**
  - `file.IndexOf("/roslyn")` -> offset 10 instead of 9 (ignorable `/`)
  - `compilerVersionStart` -> offset 17 (pointing at `.`)
  - `file.IndexOf('/', 17)` -> matches immediately at 17 (ignorable `.` and `/` collision in linguistic collation)
  - Extracted version substring -> `""` (Length 0)
  - `Version.TryParse("")` fails -> All analyzer variants (`roslyn4.0` .. `roslyn5.0`) loaded -> Build fails with `CS0111`
- **After:**
  - `file.IndexOf("/roslyn", StringComparison.Ordinal)` -> offset 9
  - `compilerVersionStart` -> offset 16 (pointing at `5`)
  - `file.IndexOf('/', 16)` -> offset 19
  - Extracted version substring -> `"5.0"`
  - `Version.TryParse("5.0")` succeeds -> Only the highest compatible Roslyn analyzer is selected.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** two-way
**Blast Radius:** low (internal path resolution helper; technical paths must always use Ordinal string comparison per .NET runtime guidelines).

Issues.Title: --coverage-output flag silently omits/deletes output files when solution has multiple test projects
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

If `dotnet test --coverage` is run with the flag `--coverage-output` in a solution with multiple test projects, there will be a report from only one of the test projects

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a solution with two test projects using MTP
2. Run `dotnet test --coverage --coverage-output-format cobertura --coverage-output my-output-file.xml `
3. Inspect the output

Minimal demo: https://github.com/computaserik/CoverageOutputDemo/tree/main

### Expected behavior

`dotnet test` should fail, or at least issue a clear warning that output will be missing.

### Actual behavior

The test reports from all but one of the projects are silently omitted/deleted.

### Is this a regression?

_No response_

### Are there any workarounds?

Remove the `--coverage-output` option.

```console

```

### IDE version

_No response_

Issues.Title: .NET October 2026 out-of-band security updates
Issues.Body:
On October 25, 2026, we released out-of-band security updates for .NET 8.0.33, .NET 9.0.22, .NET 10.0.14, and .NET 11 Release Candidate 3 (prerelease). We recommend updating affected applications and build environments as soon as possible. .NET Framework is not affected.

## Release Notes

* [Release details and feedback](https://github.com/dotnet/core/issues/10660)
* [.NET 8.0.33 and .NET SDK 8.0.133 / 8.0.427](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/8.0/8.0.33/8.0.33.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/8.0))
* [.NET 9.0.22 and .NET SDK 9.0.123 / 9.0.320](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/9.0/9.0.22/9.0.22.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/9.0))
* [.NET 10.0.14 and .NET SDK 10.0.114 / 10.0.403](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/10.0/10.0.14/10.0.14.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/10.0))
* [.NET 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 and .NET SDK 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 (prerelease)](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc3/11.0.0-rc.3.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/11.0))

## Security advisories

| Advisory | Applicability | Announcement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [CVE-2026-111497](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/security/advisories/GHSA-p3jp-9v83-76w9) | Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write; all platforms when processing untrusted Brotli data. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494) |
| [CVE-2026-114148](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/security/advisories/GHSA-r6pf-x897-gm86) | Linux archive ownership; distribution-specific ASP.NET Core archives and source-build engineering inputs. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/495) |
| [CVE-2026-70197](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/security/advisories/GHSA-4mpw-cpwj-hxxj) | Windows sockets memory corruption; corrected October 13 fix. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/493) |
| [CVE-2026-102870](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/security/advisories/GHSA-g27p-qf6j-c96c) | Standalone Blazor WebAssembly debugger packages on .NET 10/11; corrected October 13 fix. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/492) |

The October 13 updates did not fully address CVE-2026-70197 and CVE-2026-102870. These out-of-band updates provide the corrected fixes; the original advisory identities and revision history are preserved. For CVE-2026-102870, update the affected standalone Server/DevServer package references; updating only the shared runtime is not a substitute.

For CVE-2026-114148, affected Microsoft-published .NET 8/9 ASP.NET Core runtime and targeting-pack tarball installations require a clean replacement following the advisory. Source-built archives are build/engineering inputs, not directly deployed production runtimes. Update those inputs and recreate their extracted workspaces using ownership-controlled extraction; review and rebuild affected downstream outputs as needed. .NET 10/11 applicability is limited to source-built distributions.

Also announced at [.NET October 2026 Out-of-Band Security Updates](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/dotnet-october-2026-oob-security-updates/).

Please use the [release feedback issue](https://github.com/dotnet/core/issues/10660) for release-wide issues and the linked per-CVE discussions for advisory questions.

Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-114148 | .NET Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in file ownership in Linux .NET tarball distributions, including ASP.NET Core runtime tarballs, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack tarballs, and source-built .NET tarballs. This advisory also provides guidance on updating affected installations and source-build engineering workflows. Incorrect ownership of runtime files installed from affected Linux tarballs can allow local elevation of privilege. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/70040 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 7.8 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-276 (Incorrect Default Permissions) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Linux - **Architectures:** ARM, ARM64 and x64, as applicable to the affected Linux distribution. ## Affected Products The affected ASP.NET Core runtime, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack, and source-built .NET Linux tarballs are listed below. The installation and source-build engineering scenarios require different remediation, as described in [How do I fix the issue?](#how-fix). ### Microsoft-published ASP.NET Core archives For Microsoft-published .NET 8 and .NET 9 distributions, only the ASP.NET Core runtime and targeting-pack tarballs are affected. Other Microsoft-published .NET runtime and SDK tarballs are not included in this scope. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- ASP.NET Core 8 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 8 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 9 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 ASP.NET Core 9 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 These products use the archive names `aspnetcore-runtime-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, `aspnetcore-runtime-composite-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, and `aspnetcore-targeting-pack-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, where `{rid}` is `linux-arm`, `linux-arm64`, `linux-x64`, `linux-musl-arm`, `linux-musl-arm64` or `linux-musl-x64`. Runtime tarballs are listed on the [.NET download site](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet); targeting-pack tarballs are distributed through the .NET download CDN. ### Source-built distributions Every tarball type produced by source-build is affected in the ranges below, not only SDK tarballs. The versions in this table identify the corresponding source-build SDK release. Source-built tarballs are used in build and engineering workflows, rather than deployed directly to customer installations. Consuming an affected source-build archive does not, by itself, mean that a production shared runtime was installed from that archive. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- Source-built .NET 8 Linux distributions | >= 8.0.100, < 8.0.133 | 8.0.133 Source-built .NET 9 Linux distributions | >= 9.0.100, < 9.0.123 | 9.0.123 Source-built .NET 10.0.1xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.100, <= 10.0.113 | 10.0.114-servicing.26522.126 Source-built .NET 10.0.4xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.400, <= 10.0.402 | 10.0.403-servicing.26523.112 Source-built .NET 11 preview Linux distributions | >= 11.0.100-preview.1.26104.118, <= 11.0.100-rc.2.26504.105 | 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Review whether an installation came from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, or whether a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built archive. Check whether extraction preserved numeric ownership and whether the resulting files have the intended ownership. A .NET version number alone does not identify which archive was used or establish the ownership of an installation or build workspace. The vulnerability can affect installations that preserve numeric file ownership from an affected archive, for example during privileged extraction or ownership-preserving container archive import. A local account that controls the installed files or writable directories may be able to modify files used by a more privileged application. Restoring ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack NuGet packages does not, by itself, introduce this tarball ownership defect. Applications using a shared runtime installed from an affected tarball can still be affected. ### How do I fix the issue? #### Customer-deployed installations For an installation made from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, replace the affected installation with a clean installation from the patched distribution listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Updating a NuGet reference, downloading a new archive, or extracting over an existing installation does not by itself correct the existing installation. 1. Identify the affected installation directories and the applications, services, scheduled jobs, and container images that use them. Stop affected applications and services before switching installations. 2. Obtain the patched archives appropriate to your distribution, architecture, and required components from the trusted publisher. Verify their checksums against the publisher's trusted release information before extracting them. 3. Install into a **new, empty directory**, not the affected installation tree. For a shared or privileged installation, use a trusted administrator account and an administrator-controlled directory whose parent directories cannot be modified by untrusted accounts. Do not copy binaries, plugins, or other files from the affected tree into the replacement. Install any required side-by-side versions from trusted, fixed distributions. 4. Extract without restoring the archive's user/group ownership. Follow the [manual installation guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/install/linux-scripted-manual#manual-install), which uses `--no-same-owner`. For GNU tar, the following example also applies a restrictive write-permission mask: ```bash ( umask 022 tar -xzf "$PATCHED_ARCHIVE" -C "$NEW_DOTNET_ROOT" \ --no-same-owner --no-same-permissions ) ``` `PATCHED_ARCHIVE` must identify the verified patched archive, and `NEW_DOTNET_ROOT` must identify the new, empty installation directory. For a shared or privileged installation, run extraction in the trusted administrator context. Confirm that the resulting files, directories, and parent directories are controlled by the intended trusted owner and cannot be modified by untrusted accounts, including through group permissions or access-control lists. 5. Update application and service configuration to use the replacement installation, then restart and verify the applications. Check the actual runtime selected by each application, not only the version reported by an unrelated `dotnet` executable on `PATH`. Ensure that no service, scheduled job, or runtime search path still selects the affected installation. Retire the old tree using your deployment procedures, preserving evidence first if compromise is suspected. 6. Rebuild affected custom container images from trusted inputs using the patched archives and ownership-controlled extraction, and deploy replacement containers. Changing only a running container does not correct the image used to create subsequent containers. #### Source-build engineering workflows If a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built tarball, update that input to the patched source-build release listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Recreate its extracted workspace in a new, trusted directory using ownership-controlled extraction, rather than reusing a tree extracted from the affected archive. The extraction guidance above also applies to these workspaces. Review downstream runtime or SDK packages and custom images for ownership inherited from the affected archive, and rebuild affected outputs as needed. The customer-installation steps above apply if affected outputs were actually installed or deployed; do not treat the source-build engineering archive itself as a deployed production runtime. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 | .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136446 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Mitigations ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths: - Enable ASP.NET Core [automatic request decompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-decompression) with Brotli (`br`) support. - Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring [HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclienthandler.automaticdecompression) or [SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.socketshttphandler.automaticdecompression) to include [DecompressionMethods.Brotli](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.decompressionmethods) or `DecompressionMethods.All`. - Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in `System.IO.Compression`, such as `BrotliStream` or `BrotliDecoder`. Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data. The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it. > **Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression.** Do not introduce a call to `AddRequestDecompression` if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an `AutomaticDecompression` property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded. If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the `br` entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers: ```csharp builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options => { options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br"); }); ``` If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include `DecompressionMethods.Brotli`: ```csharp var handler = new HttpClientHandler { AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate }; var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler); ``` Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages See [mitigations](#mitigations) for the affected usage paths and default settings. ### How do I fix the issue? Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above. .NET release | Runtime | SDK versions ------------ | ------- | ------------ .NET 8 | 8.0.33 | 8.0.133, 8.0.427 .NET 9 | 9.0.22 | 9.0.123, 9.0.320 .NET 10 | 10.0.14 | 10.0.114, 10.0.403 .NET 11 previews | 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 | 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet. * If you're using .NET 8.0, you should download and install .NET 8.0.33 Runtime or .NET 8.0.133 or 8.0.427 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/8.0. * If you're using .NET 9.0, you should download and install .NET 9.0.22 Runtime or .NET 9.0.123 or 9.0.320 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/9.0. * If you're using .NET 10.0, you should download and install .NET 10.0.14 Runtime or .NET 10.0.114 or 10.0.403 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/10.0. * If you're using .NET 11.0, you should download and install .NET 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 Runtime or .NET 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/11.0. For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-70197 | .NET and Visual Studio Remote Code Execution Vulnerability | October 25, 2026 OOB update
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in System.Net.Sockets. This advisory also provides guidance on what developers can do to update their applications to remove this vulnerability. On Windows, reusing a `SocketAsyncEventArgs` instance across IPv4 and IPv6 datagram sockets can retain an undersized cached native address buffer, allowing an unauthenticated out-of-bounds write during `ReceiveFromAsync`. This vulnerability was disclosed in the October 13 advisory, but the fix was not included in the previous updates. This revision provides the corrected packages under the existing CVE-2026-70197. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136445 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Windows - **Architectures:** All ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects Microsoft .NET projects that use an affected package version listed below. [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.win-x86](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.win-x86) | >= 10.0.0, < 10.0.14 | 10.0.14 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? If using a package listed in [affected packages](#affected-packages), you're exposed to the vulnerability. The affected .NET 8 Windows packages include both CoreCLR and Mono runtime packs. The issue requires reuse of `SocketAsyncEventArgs` across IPv4 and IPv6 datagram sockets; it is not limited to one runtime implementation. ### How do I fix the issue? 1. To fix the issue please install the latest version of .NET. If you have installed one or more .NET SDKs through Visual Studio, Visual Studio will prompt you to update Visual Studio, which will also update your .NET SDKs. 2. If your application references the vulnerable package, update the package reference to the patched version. You can list the versions you have installed by running the `dotnet --info` command. * If you're using .NET 8.0, you should download and install .NET 8.0.33 Runtime or .NET 8.0.133 or 8.0.427 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/8.0. * If you're using .NET 9.0, you should download and install .NET 9.0.22 Runtime or .NET 9.0.123 or 9.0.320 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/9.0. * If you're using .NET 10.0, you should download and install .NET 10.0.14 Runtime or .NET 10.0.114 or 10.0.403 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/10.0. * If you're using .NET 11.0, you should download and install .NET 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 Runtime or .NET 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/11.0. Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect. Additionally, if you've deployed [self-contained applications](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/deploying/#self-contained-deployments-scd) targeting any of the impacted versions, these applications are also vulnerable and must be recompiled and redeployed. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-102870 | ASP.NET Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability | October 25, 2026 OOB update
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in the Blazor WebAssembly debugger included in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server`. This advisory also provides guidance on what developers can do to update their applications to remove this vulnerability. `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer` also bundles the affected debugger. The Blazor WebAssembly debug proxy evaluates debugger expressions by generating and compiling C# source. Certain values originating in the application being debugged, including `ToString()` results, descriptions, and class names, are embedded in that generated source without consistent escaping. An attacker-controlled value can escape the generated string literal and execute code on a developer's machine when the developer evaluates an expression during debugging. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/70039 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.8 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-94 (Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Windows, Linux, macOS - **Architectures:** All ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects Microsoft .NET projects that use an affected package version listed below. Package name | Affected version | Patched version ------------ | ---------------- | --------------- [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server) | >= 10.0.0, < 10.0.14 | 10.0.14 [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server) | >= 11.0.0-preview.1, < 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 | 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer) | >= 10.0.0, < 10.0.14 | 10.0.14 [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer) | >= 11.0.0-preview.1, < 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 | 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? You are affected if you use a vulnerable version of `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server` or `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer` to debug a Blazor WebAssembly application and evaluate an expression involving attacker-controlled application data. ### How do I fix the issue? 1. Install the latest supported version of .NET. 2. Update each affected `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server` or `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer` package reference to the patched version for the .NET release used by the application. Updating only the shared runtime is not a substitute for updating these standalone packages. Once the updated packages are installed, restart the debugger and development environment. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repositories are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime and https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore. The Announcements repository (https://github.com/dotnet/announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. ### Disclaimer The information provided in this advisory is provided "as is" without warranty of any kind. Microsoft disclaims all warranties, either express or implied, including the warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose. In no event shall Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers be liable for any damages whatsoever including direct, indirect, incidental, consequential, loss of business profits or special damages, even if Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers have been advised of the possibility of such damages. Some states do not allow the exclusion or limitation of liability for consequential or incidental damages so the foregoing limitation may not apply. ### External Links [CVE-2026-102870](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-102870) ### Acknowledgements - alittleston3 ### Revisions V1.0 (10/13/2026): Advisory published. Issues.Title: .NET 11 Release Candidate 2
Issues.Body:
> This issue is a locked mirror of [dotnet/core/discussions/10644](https://github.com/dotnet/core/discussions/10644). See that thread for discussion.

We are pleased to announce the release of .NET 11 Release Candidate 2. Follow the main announcement and [blog announcement](https://aka.ms/dotnet/11/rc2).

This is our second of two release candidates which come with a [go-live support license](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/platform/support/policy/dotnet-core#previews) so you can confidently use this release for your production applications. This release of .NET 11 is supported in the new [Visual Studio 2026 Insiders](https://visualstudio.microsoft.com/insiders/) release alongside Visual Studio Code with the C# Dev Kit. Check out the full release notes below and get started today.

This release contains the following highlights and improvements.

Browse the release notes for a full list of improvements in this release:

- [.NET MAUI](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/dotnetmaui.md)
- [ASP.NET Core](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/aspnetcore.md)
- [C#](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/csharp.md)
- [F#](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/fsharp.md)
- [Container images](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/containers.md)

ASP.NET Core request-localization fallback can add attacker-supplied synthetic culture names to the runtime's global cache, allowing unauthenticated requests to cause unbounded memory growth and denial of service. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/69803 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 7.5 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` - **Weakness:** CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Windows, Linux, macOS - **Architectures:** All ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects Microsoft .NET projects that use an affected package version listed below. If you have installed one or more .NET SDKs through Visual Studio, Visual Studio will prompt you to update Visual Studio, which will also update your .NET SDKs. 2. If your application references the vulnerable package, update the package reference to the patched version. You can list the versions you have installed by running the `dotnet --info` command. * If you're using .NET 8.0, you should download and install .NET 8.0.32 Runtime or .NET 8.0.426 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/8.0. * If you're using .NET 9.0, you should download and install .NET 9.0.21 Runtime or .NET 9.0.319 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/9.0. * If you're using .NET 10.0, you should download and install .NET 10.0.13 Runtime or .NET 10.0.402 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/10.0. * If you're using .NET 11.0, you should download and install .NET 11.0.0-rc.2 Runtime or .NET 11.0.100-rc.2 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/11.0. Issues.Body: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime; System.Private.CoreLib. This advisory also provides guidance on what developers can do to update their applications to remove this vulnerability. If using a package listed in [affected packages](#affected-packages), you're exposed to the vulnerability. ### How do I fix the issue? 1. To fix the issue please install the latest version of .NET. If you have installed one or more .NET SDKs through Visual Studio, Visual Studio will prompt you to update Visual Studio, which will also update your .NET SDKs. 2. If your application references the vulnerable package, update the package reference to the patched version. You can list the versions you have installed by running the `dotnet --info` command. * If you're using .NET 8.0, you should download and install .NET 8.0.32 Runtime or .NET 8.0.426 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/8.0. * If you're using .NET 9.0, you should download and install .NET 9.0.21 Runtime or .NET 9.0.319 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/9.0. * If you're using .NET 10.0, you should download and install .NET 10.0.13 Runtime or .NET 10.0.402 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/10.0. * If you're using .NET 11.0, you should download and install .NET 11.0.0-rc.2 Runtime or .NET 11.0.100-rc.2 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/11.0. Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.
